title: Morris v. Commissioner, New Hampshire Department of Revenue Administration
description: Whether Robert and Mary Morris were residents of New Hampshire for tax purposes and whether New Hampshire's interest and dividends tax scheme violates state and federal constitutions.
plaintiff_argument: The Morrises argued they were not New Hampshire residents for tax purposes, the state's interest and dividends tax resulted in unconstitutional double taxation, and it violated the dormant Commerce Clause.
defendant_argument: The New Hampshire Department of Revenue Administration argued the Morrises were residents based on their actions and the state's tax scheme was constitutional.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's decision, finding the Morrises were residents of New Hampshire for tax purposes and upholding the tax assessment, penalties, and denial of attorney's fees.

title: City of Dover v. Secretary of State
description: Whether the decennial redistricting plan (RSA 662:5) violates Part II, Article 11 of the New Hampshire Constitution by failing to maximize the number of towns and wards with dedicated districts.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that Part II, Article 11 of the New Hampshire Constitution requires the Legislature to maximize dedicated districts and that the enacted plan lacked a rational or legitimate basis for not doing so.
defendant_argument: The defendants countered that legislative policy preferences provide a rational basis for the plan, as full compliance with all constitutional requirements is impossible, and the court should not substitute its judgment for the Legislature's political decision.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Superior Court's decision, upholding the constitutionality of the decennial redistricting plan (RSA 662:5) and ruling that the plaintiffs failed to demonstrate a lack of rational or legitimate basis for its enactment.

title: State v. Zarella
description: Whether the constitutional right to privacy, as established by N.H. Const. Part I, Art. 2-B, changes the standard a criminal defendant must meet to obtain in camera review and disclosure of confidential counseling and mental health records held by private organizations.
plaintiff_argument: The complainant and the State argued that Part I, Article 2-b abrogates the prior standard (Cressey's application of Gagne) and requires a heightened standard for obtaining in camera review and disclosure of confidential or privileged records held by private organizations.
defendant_argument: The defendant contended that Part I, Article 2-b does not alter the existing Gagne standard for obtaining in camera review and disclosure of confidential or privileged records.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that Part I, Article 2-b of the State Constitution abrogates the prior standard (Cressey's application of Gagne) for records held by private organizations, requiring a higher "essential need" standard for certain records and the RSA 173-C:5 procedure for others, and vacated the trial court's order denying the complainant's motion to quash.

title: In re Doe
description: Whether the New Hampshire Board of Medicine violated John Doe's due process rights or acted arbitrarily by refusing to remove records of his temporary license suspension from its website after the suspension was vacated and he surrendered his license.
plaintiff_argument: Doe argued that the Board violated his due process rights by temporarily suspending his license ex parte and then refusing to remove the related documents from its website, which negatively affected him professionally and personally. He also asserted that the Board's actions were arbitrary and capricious.
defendant_argument: The Board contended that Doe waived any due process claim, that it acted within its statutory responsibility to protect the public, and that the posting of orders is consistent with public records laws and its obligation to ensure public access to disciplinary actions.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Board's decision not to remove all references to the emergency suspension order and related documents from its website and Doe's physician profile.

title: Contoocook Valley School District v. New Hampshire
description: Whether the State has fulfilled its constitutional obligation to determine the cost of, and sufficiently fund, the opportunity for a constitutionally adequate education for each educable child in New Hampshire, with plaintiffs arguing it has not and defendants arguing it has or that the court's intervention is improper.
plaintiff_argument: The State's base adequacy aid is constitutionally insufficient to cover the cost of providing an adequate education, and the State failed to justify its funding level under strict scrutiny.
defendant_argument: The trial court's methodology was flawed, the plaintiffs failed to provide sufficient evidence, and the immediate funding directive violates the separation of powers doctrine.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's declaration that RSA 198:40-a, II(a) is facially unconstitutional and that the State has not fulfilled its constitutional obligation to fund an adequate education, but reversed the trial court's directive that the State immediately increase public school funding.

title: Attorney General v. Hood
description: Whether the trial court erred by requiring the State to prove 'knowing' trespass to avoid an unconstitutionally overbroad application of the Civil Rights Act, thereby dismissing the State's complaints.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that its broader interpretation of the Civil Rights Act, without a 'knowing' trespass requirement, was constitutional and not overbroad or vague, and that its complaints sufficiently alleged civil trespass.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the State's interpretation of the Civil Rights Act was unconstitutionally overbroad and vague, infringing on free speech, and that a 'knowing' trespass requirement was necessary to protect constitutional rights.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's dismissal, ruling that the State's construction of the Civil Rights Act was unconstitutional due to overbreadth and vagueness, and that the Act requires proof of 'knowing' trespass, which the State failed to allege.

title: In re Port City Air Leasing, Inc.
description: Whether Port City Air Leasing, Inc. has standing as a "landowner" or "person aggrieved" under state statutes to appeal a wetlands permit decision, and whether denying such standing violates its state and federal due process rights.
plaintiff_argument: Port City argues it is an "abutting landowner" and thus a "person aggrieved" entitled to appeal the wetlands permit decision, and that denying it standing violates its state and federal due process rights by depriving it of a remedy and a pre-deprivation hearing.
defendant_argument: Million Air counters that Port City is not a "landowner" because its interests in the leased premises are not equivalent to fee ownership, and therefore Port City lacks standing.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Hearing Officer's dismissal of Port City's appeal, concluding that Port City lacks standing under the relevant statutes and that this construction does not violate its state or federal due process rights.

title: Richard v. Governor
description: Whether the State Constitution mandates hand-counting of votes and whether statutes authorizing electronic voting machines are unconstitutional, including if their discretionary use violates equal protection.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argues that Part II, Article 32 of the State Constitution mandates hand-counting of votes, making statutes authorizing electronic voting machines unconstitutional, and that the discretionary use of electronic voting machines violates equal protection by creating an unequal election process.
defendant_argument: The defendants argue that the State Constitution does not mandate hand-counting of votes, allowing the legislature to authorize electronic voting machines, and that the plaintiff's claims regarding electronic voting machines and equal protection do not demonstrate a concrete, personal injury.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the dismissal of the plaintiff's claim that the State Constitution mandates hand-counting of votes, but remanded the plaintiff's equal protection claim regarding electronic voting machines for further proceedings, and dismissed the remaining claims (III-VI) for lack of standing.

title: State v. Diole
description: Whether RSA 135-E:5 violates due process and equal protection by denying incompetent defendants a jury trial, rules of evidence, and medical privilege in civil commitment proceedings, protections afforded to competent defendants.
plaintiff_argument: The State argues that the purpose of RSA 135-E:5 hearings is not to adjudicate guilt but to determine if the person committed the acts as part of qualifying them as a sexually violent predator for public protection and treatment, and that the differing goals of criminal prosecution and civil commitment justify the disparate treatment.
defendant_argument: Amuri Diole argues that RSA 135-E:5 violates due process by allowing 'conviction' without a jury trial, denying rules of evidence and medical privilege, and allowing 'conviction' based on propensity evidence. He also argues it violates equal protection by treating incompetent defendants differently from competent ones regarding these protections.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's order, ruling that RSA 135-E:5 does not violate due process or equal protection under the State and Federal Constitutions.

title: State v. Warren
description: Whether permitting a victim to testify at trial via a one-way livestream video feed outside the defendant's presence violated the defendant's constitutional right to meet witnesses "face to face."
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that allowing the child victim to testify via one-way video feed was necessary to prevent trauma and ensure reliable testimony, as the child would be under oath, cross-examined, and her demeanor observable by the jury, judge, and defendant.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that allowing the child victim to testify outside her presence via video feed violated her right to face-to-face confrontation under the New Hampshire Constitution.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the first-degree assault conviction and reversed the second-degree assault conviction, remanding the case.

title: Jane Doe v. Manchester School District
description: Whether a public school policy that allows school personnel to not disclose a student's transgender status or gender nonconforming presentation to parents, without the student's consent, violates a parent's constitutional parenting rights.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argues that the school district's policy violates her constitutional parenting rights by encouraging school officials to conceal her child's gender identity transition in school from her.
defendant_argument: The defendants argue that the policy is constitutional, does not infringe upon a fundamental parental right, and survives rational basis review.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the trial court's order granting the defendants' motion to dismiss, finding that the policy does not infringe upon a fundamental parenting right.

title: Hardy v. Chester Arms, LLC
description: Whether firearms seller Chester Arms, LLC and the New Hampshire Department of Safety are immune from liability for negligent entrustment and negligence per se, and whether the state immunity statutes (RSA 508:21 and RSA 541-B:19) are constitutional or preempted by federal law.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that Chester Arms waived its immunity, that RSA 508:21 only provides immunity if harm is solely caused by criminal use, that the statute is preempted by federal law, and that it violates state constitutional rights to a remedy and equal protection. They also argued that the Department of Safety was not immune because it failed to exercise due care and MacPherson was federally disqualified from owning a firearm.
defendant_argument: Chester Arms argued that immunity under RSA 508:21 is a jurisdictional issue and cannot be waived, that the statute provides complete immunity for damages resulting from criminal misuse, that it is not preempted by federal law, and that it is constitutional as it protects the right to bear arms. The Department of Safety argued it was immune, and alternatively, that MacPherson was not federally disqualified, making any immunity error harmless.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's grant of summary judgment, finding both Chester Arms, LLC and the New Hampshire Department of Safety immune from suit.

title: Brown v. Secretary of State
description: Whether claims of extreme partisan gerrymandering are justiciable under the New Hampshire Constitution, with plaintiffs arguing they are and the defendant arguing they are not.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argue that the legislature violated the New Hampshire Constitution by drawing districts that unfairly benefit one political party, and that their claims of partisan gerrymandering are justiciable under various articles of the State Constitution, which provide discernible and manageable standards for judicial intervention.
defendant_argument: The defendant argues that the plaintiffs' claims present non-justiciable political questions because the State Constitution textually commits redistricting authority exclusively to the Legislature and lacks discoverable and manageable standards for judicial intervention regarding partisan gerrymandering.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's dismissal, holding that claims of partisan gerrymandering present a non-justiciable political question under the New Hampshire Constitution.

title: State v. O'Brien
description: Whether an officer unlawfully expanded the scope of a traffic stop, initiated for a defective license plate light, by requesting consent to search the vehicle for drugs based solely on the odor of marijuana.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the officer's observation of the defective license plate light provided a lawful basis for the stop, and the odor of marijuana provided reasonable, articulable suspicion to expand the scope of the stop and ask for consent to search.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the officer unlawfully expanded the scope of the stop beyond the initial traffic violation by asking for consent to search for drugs, as the mere odor of marijuana alone did not provide reasonable, articulable suspicion for a drug crime, thus tainting her consent.
decision_outcome: The court concluded that the trial court erred in denying the defendant's motion to suppress, reversed the convictions, and remanded the case.

title: In re Smart
description: Whether the executive branch's discretionary exercise of clemency power, specifically regarding a commutation hearing, is subject to judicial review and mandamus, or if it constitutes a nonjusticiable political question.
plaintiff_argument: The petitioner argues that the Governor and Executive Council acted arbitrarily and in bad faith by denying her commutation hearing, violating her constitutional right to demonstrate fitness to return to society and minimal due process.
defendant_argument: The State argues the court lacks jurisdiction because the petitioner raises a nonjusticiable political question regarding the executive branch's clemency power, which is committed to a coordinate political department.
decision_outcome: The court dismissed the petition for lack of jurisdiction, ruling that the executive branch's exercise of clemency power is a nonjusticiable political question and not subject to judicial review.

title: In re New Hampshire Divison for Children, Youth & Families
description: Whether RSA 508:8, which allows minors or mentally incompetent persons to bring a personal action within 2 years after their disability is removed, applies to claims brought against the State under RSA chapter 541-B, which has a 3-year statute of limitations.
plaintiff_argument: The New Hampshire Division for Children, Youth and Families (DCYF) argued that RSA 508:8 does not apply to claims under RSA chapter 541-B, asserting that the three-year limitation period in 541-B:14, IV is constitutional as applied to child plaintiffs and does not violate equal protection.
defendant_argument: The respondent argued that RSA 508:8 must be read into RSA 541-B:14, IV to ensure the statute complies with the equal protection guarantees of the New Hampshire Constitution, preventing a class of children from being unfairly barred from recourse against the State.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's decision, ruling that RSA 508:8 must be read into RSA 541-B:14, IV to ensure equal protection for child plaintiffs, thereby denying DCYF's motion to dismiss.

title: Mallard v. Warden, New Hampshire State Prison
description: Whether Marc Mallard's trial counsel provided ineffective assistance by making racially biased remarks during cross-examination, thereby prejudicing the trial outcome, and whether his habeas corpus petition was procedurally barred.
plaintiff_argument: Mallard argued that his trial counsel's reference to him as a "big, menacing black guy" constituted ineffective assistance of counsel, infected his trial with racial bias, and prejudiced the jury, and that his habeas petition was not procedurally barred.
defendant_argument: The Warden argued that Mallard's habeas petition was procedurally barred because he had previously litigated ineffective assistance claims, and that the racial reference was a single, fleeting remark that did not cause prejudice.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the Superior Court's dismissal of Mallard's habeas petition, finding that his trial counsel's performance was constitutionally deficient and prejudiced the outcome of the trial, and remanded the case for further proceedings.

title: State v. Verrill
description: Whether the Double Jeopardy and Due Process Clauses of the State and Federal Constitutions prohibit the defendant's retrial following the State's significant discovery violations and a granted mistrial.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that its discovery violations were not intentional or malicious, but rather the product of sloppiness and poor management, and that remedies short of dismissal with prejudice were sufficient to cure any potential prejudice, thus retrial is not barred.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the State's conduct amounted to either intentional goading for a mistrial or reckless disregard/gross negligence in discovery, causing severe prejudice that could only be cured by dismissal with prejudice.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's denial of the defendant's motion to dismiss the indictments with prejudice, allowing retrial, but vacated the denial of the defendant's motion for additional factual findings and remanded for further proceedings.

title: State v. Donovan
description: Whether the trial court erred in denying the defendant's motion to suppress evidence, specifically whether the defendant was subjected to an unlawful seizure without reasonable suspicion before incriminating evidence was discovered.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that any questioning did not exceed the scope of the initial stop, or that the stop was lawful under the community caretaking exception, and that the investigatory stop was not impermissibly expanded.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that he was seized without reasonable suspicion when his passenger was asked to exit the vehicle and his identification was retained, making all subsequently discovered evidence the fruit of an illegal seizure.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the trial court's denial of the defendant's motion to suppress evidence, concluding that the defendant's seizure violated his rights under the State Constitution.

title: In re State
description: Whether the Governor's actions of sending an email to state employees regarding collective bargaining negotiations and refusing to submit a fact-finder's report to the Executive Council constituted unfair labor practices.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the Governor's email did not interfere with employee rights or union business, and that he was not required to submit a rejected fact-finder's report to the Executive Council, thus his actions were not unfair labor practices.
defendant_argument: The PELRB and Unions argued that the Governor's email constituted direct dealing and interfered with union rights, and that he was legally obligated to submit the fact-finder's report to the Executive Council, making his refusal an unfair labor practice.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the PELRB's decision, concluding that the State did not commit unfair labor practices.

title: Richard v. Speaker of the House of Representatives
description: Whether the New Hampshire Constitution requires the legislature to hold a public hearing on a citizen's remonstrances.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that Part I, Articles 31 and 32, along with other constitutional provisions, mandate the legislature to assemble and hold a public hearing on his remonstrances to redress grievances.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the controversy was nonjusticiable and that the New Hampshire Constitution does not require the legislature to hold hearings on remonstrances.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's dismissal of the plaintiff's complaint, finding no constitutional mandate for the legislature to hold a public hearing on a citizen's remonstrance.

title: State v. Davis
description: Whether evidence obtained during warrantless entries into a residence and a subsequent search warrant predicated on that evidence should be suppressed.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that both warrantless entries into the defendant's residence were lawful, and therefore, the later search warrant based on those entries was also lawful.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the warrantless entry into his enclosed porch was unlawful because he had a legitimate expectation of privacy, the subsequent warrantless entry into the mobile home was not justified by exigent circumstances, and the search warrant was invalid as it relied on unlawfully obtained evidence.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the lower court's decision and remanded the case, concluding that all evidence obtained during the two warrantless entries and the evidence seized pursuant to the search warrant should have been suppressed.

title: State v. Hinkley
description: Whether Officer Marsh's statements to the defendant constituted a promise of immunity, rendering the defendant's confession involuntary under the State Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the trial court erred in suppressing the defendant's confession, contending that Officer Marsh's statements were accurate statements of fact about the age of consent, not promises of immunity, and that the confession was not induced by them.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that his confession was involuntary because Officer Marsh's statements constituted an unqualified promise of immunity from prosecution, and he relied on that promise when confessing.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the trial court's ruling, suppressing the defendant's confession and all subsequent statements, finding them to be per se involuntary under the New Hampshire Constitution.

title: Carrigan v. New Hampshire Department of Health & Human Services
description: Whether Part I, Article 8 of the New Hampshire Constitution grants taxpayers standing to challenge a governmental body's overall spending policies or only specific governmental spending actions.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the Department's 'irresponsible' spending decisions regarding child welfare violated statutory and constitutional duties, and that Part I, Article 8 grants taxpayers standing to challenge such overall spending policies.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that taxpayer standing under Part I, Article 8 is limited to challenging specific, identifiable expenditures or approvals, and does not extend to broad challenges of a governmental body's general spending policies.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's grant of the defendants' motion to dismiss, ruling that the plaintiff lacked standing.

title: New Hampshire Democratic Party v. Secretary of State
description: Whether Senate Bill 3, which amends New Hampshire's voter registration laws, unconstitutionally burdens the right to vote and violates equal protection guarantees of the State Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that SB 3's procedural requirements, associated penalties, and incomprehensibility severely and unreasonably burden the fundamental right to vote, and there is no governmental interest to justify these burdens.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the trial court erred in invalidating SB 3, asserting that the law does not unconstitutionally burden the right to vote and is justified by the state's interest in preventing wrongful voting and voter fraud.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's ruling that Senate Bill 3 is unconstitutional because it imposes unreasonable burdens on the right to vote and the State failed to demonstrate it was substantially related to an important governmental objective.

title: In re M.M.
description: Whether the July 2020 amendment to RSA 169-C:28, which eliminated de novo review for final dispositional orders in abuse and neglect proceedings, applies to Father's case, and whether there was sufficient evidence to support the circuit court's finding of neglect against Father.
plaintiff_argument: DCYF argues that the July 2020 amendment to RSA 169-C:28 applies to Father's case, barring his appeal to the superior court for de novo review, and that there was sufficient evidence to support the finding of neglect.
defendant_argument: Father argues that the July 2020 amendment to RSA 169-C:28 should not apply to his case because his right to de novo appeal vested upon filing, and that the circuit court should not have considered DCYF's neglect petition or, alternatively, there was insufficient evidence to support the neglect finding.
decision_outcome: The court concluded that the July 2020 amendment to RSA 169-C:28 applies to Father's case, barring his appeal to the superior court for de novo review, and affirmed the circuit court's finding of neglect against Father.
